newsitem.title: USA: Health commandos arrive at Nebraska beef plant.
newsitem.headline: Health commandos arrive at Nebraska beef plant.

text.p: A team of inspectors from the U.S. Agriculture Department descended on a Nebraska meat plant at sunrise Monday looking for the cause of the recall of 5 million hamburger patties, department officials said.
The investigative team included representatives from the department's inspector general's office. They are seeking to determine whether criminal charges are warranted.

Susan Conley, spokeswoman for the department's Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS), said investigators arrived at 6 a.m. at the Hudson Foods plant to pore over records and check meat processing procedures.

On Friday, the department announced a record recall of ground beef due to possible contamination with a deadly strain of the E. coli bacterium. Health officials blamed the bacterium for 16 cases of illness in Colorado in July.
Five million hamburger patties or 1.2 million pounds of beef processed at a Hudson Foods plant in Columbus, Nebraska, over three days in June were recalled.
Initially, the department announced a recall of just 20,000 pounds of ground beef but that figure swelled as more information became available.

"We're going to examine all of the plant records associated with this three days of production as well as check our own inspection records to determine what the cause of this contamination was and learn from that what we need to change to prevent it from happening in the future," FSIS chief Thomas Billy said on ABC's "Good Morning America".
Conley said investigators would also examine the plants that supplied the beef to Hudson Foods, which is based in Rogers, Arkansas. She said the department was "still pinning down" the suppliers.
Hudson Foods officials have raised the possibility that the source of the suspected E. coli contamination was beef coming into the plant.

The company's chief financial officer, Charles Jurgensmeyer said in an interview no customers had cancelled orders due to the recall. Hudson distributes to major chains such as Burger King Corp, Boston Market, Walmart and Sam's Club.
Conley said the head of the SWAT team might report back to USDA officials in Washington later Monday but stressed the situation was still unfolding.
"This is not something you can do in a couple hours. This is something that's going to take some time," she said.
The department is in the midst of instituting revolutionary new meat inspection rules that will require testing for E.coli but these new rules will not be fully implemented for several years.
E.coli contamination occurs when the intestinal tract or feces of slaughtered animals is mixed into meat.

The strain of E.coli suspected of contaminating the beef patties can cause bloody diarrhea and dehydration, and in some, life-threatening kidney failure. The same kind of bacteria was found responsible for a fatal outbreak of disease in the Pacific Northwest in 1993.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that 10,000 to 20,000 people become infected with E. coli every year. Most cases of the foodborne illness occur when people eat undercooked ground beef or drink unpasteurized milk or sewage-contaminated water.
